claims.text: Selective dealloying of a multielement precursor alloy can produce three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Dealloying can enrich noble metals at the nanoframework surface.
The resulting noble-metal-enriched nanoframework has enhanced catalytic activity.
The precursor HEA contains noble and less-noble metals uniformly mixed at near-equiatomic ratios.
Chemical dealloying selectively dissolves the less-noble components of the HEA precursor.
Controlled acidic or alkaline dealloying can create a porous, interconnected structure without collapsing the framework.
Dealloying forms an interconnected nanoporous structure.
More-noble elements are retained during dealloying and become enriched at the surface.
Removal of less-noble elements leaves behind a three-dimensional nanoframework.
The nanoframework presents a higher density of catalytically active noble-metal sites.
A higher density of active noble-metal sites boosts catalytic performance.
The dealloyed HEA nanoframework has greater catalytic activity than the non-dealloyed HEA.
The catalytic improvement arises from increased active surface area and more efficient noble-metal utilization.
The dealloyed nanoframework may have improved stability under harsh reaction conditions.
The untreated homogeneous HEA has lower accessible surface area than the dealloyed nanoframework.
The untreated HEA has less-optimal exposure of noble-metal catalytic sites.
Effective selective dealloying requires a sufficient difference in electrochemical stability between noble and less-noble elements.
Alloy systems whose elements have only small differences in electrochemical stability may not form the desired framework morphology through selective dealloying.
